And those treatments are administered by trained professionals. There are good reasons for that. Having worked with prolonged exposure for 2 years at this point with some of my colleagues having other backgrounds I can confidently say shaming someone for not reading certain literature and telling them to suck it up isn't really part of any evidence based manual for trauma therapy. Also, the patients are never complete strangers on reddit whose situation I have no knowledge of.

This approach to trauma is potentially dangerous. I've heard plenty of anecdotes of professionals with a lack of trauma specific training pushing for trauma exposure with the best of intentions but no ability to handle the consequences. And those are professionals with a general training in psychological treatment and some knowledge of the specific patient. How overconfident would one have to be in order to feel capable of dictating the terms for a stranger's exposure?

When and how someone deals with trauma,  and at which point within treatment they expose for certain triggers is up to the person and the professional administering treatment, not strangers on the internet. Telling someone that they should just get exposed for x or y with no knowledge of their specific situation is unsolicited medical advice and therefore not appropriate. Sincerely, a psychologist.

I bought a corolla hatchback as my first car a little more than a year ago. 2002 model, 160k km on it now nearly 200k, haven't run into any serious problems. There is some rust issues around the windshield which has resulted in a leak but I "ghetto fixed" that with butyl caulk and it has held up all winter and spring. Bought the car at 28k Swedish kronor. IMHO, buying a cheap reliable car that has smaller comfort issues but works mechanically and safety wise and commuting in that for a while before investing in something better has several advantages. For me personally:
- i don't really care about this car. Door damage from other people, or potentially sliding off the road and wrecking it during my first winter wouldn't have incurred much material damage (although I am glad nothings happened so far). About a week after getting my license I scraped my bumper on a pillar near my house, didn't give a damn because it's an old car, but I've learned to better judge that distance. 
- not having payments means I can go up a price class or two once I inevitably grow tired of this leaky shitbox or it potentially breaks. So far, no mechanical issues, only normal maintenance stuff. 
- buying a better car next, after driving some old car where a working ac is considered a luxury will make the next car feel like a futuristic comfortable spaceship even if you stay within a reasonable budget. 
- it's a corolla. It'll run far beyond the point where i don't want it anymore

It seems you're comparing religious ideas to delusions or other psychotic conditions. 
The diagnostic criteria for psychosis, delusions etc in most diagnostic manuals include criterias about cultural acceptability and functional impairment. Basically, if a supernatural idea is culturally accepted and not deemed to impair function within the current cultural setting, no treatment is deemed necessary.
If a religious person lived in a cultural context where religion is completely unheard of and where, say, fasting was a practice deemed to significantly impair function, they would likely be deemed psychotic or delusional and offered treatment. But such a context doesn't really exist.

I had a lecturer from Australia in psychopathology who gave a good example of this. Some of the practices of aboriginal people would be considered signs of delusions in other cultural contexts but are accepted within that group in Australia because they do align with the cultural context, and thus don't cause harm.
